{{Short description|Iterative method in numerical analysis}}
In mathematics, '''Anderson acceleration''', also called '''Anderson mixing''', is a method for the acceleration of the convergence rate of [[fixed-point iteration]]s. Introduced by Donald G. Anderson,<ref name="Anderson1965">{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Donald G. |title=Iterative Procedures for Nonlinear Integral Equations |journal=Journal of the ACM |date=October 1965 |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=547–560 |doi=10.1145/321296.321305|doi-access=free }}</ref> this technique can be used to find the solution to fixed point equations <math>f(x) = x</math> often arising in the field of [[computational science]].

== Definition ==
Given a function <math>f:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>, consider the problem of finding a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] of <math>f</math>, which is a solution to the equation <math>f(x) = x</math>. A classical approach to the problem is to employ a [[fixed-point iteration]] scheme;<ref name="Quarteroni-Sacco">{{cite book |author-link1= Alfio Quarteroni |last1=Quarteroni |first1=Alfio |last2=Sacco |first2=Riccardo |last3=Saleri |first3=Fausto |title=Numerical mathematics |year=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-49809-4|edition=2nd}}</ref> that is, given an initial guess <math>x_0</math> for the solution, to compute the sequence <math>x_{k+1} = f(x_k)</math> until some convergence criterion is met. However, the convergence of such a scheme is not guaranteed in general; moreover, the [[rate of convergence]] is usually linear, which can become too slow if the evaluation of the function <math>f</math> is computationally expensive.<ref name="Quarteroni-Sacco" /> Anderson acceleration is a method to accelerate the convergence of the fixed-point sequence.<ref name="Quarteroni-Sacco" />

Define the residual <math>g(x) = f(x) - x</math>, and denote <math>f_k = f(x_k)</math> and <math>g_k = g(x_k)</math> (where <math>x_k</math> corresponds to the sequence of iterates from the previous paragraph). Given an initial guess <math>x_0</math> and an [[integer]] parameter <math>m \geq 1</math>, the method can be formulated as follows:<ref name="Walker2011">{{cite journal |last1=Walker |first1=Homer F. |last2=Ni |first2=Peng |title=Anderson Acceleration for Fixed-Point Iterations |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |date=January 2011 |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=1715–1735 |doi=10.1137/10078356X|citeseerx=10.1.1.722.2636 }}</ref>{{refn|group="note"|This formulation is not the same as given by the original author;<ref name="Anderson1965" /> it is an equivalent, more explicit formulation given by Walker and Ni.<ref name="Walker2011" />}}

:<math>x_1 = f(x_0)</math>

:<math>\forall k = 1, 2, \dots</math>
::<math>m_k = \min\{m, k\}</math>
::<math>G_k = \begin{bmatrix} g_{k-m_k} & \dots & g_k \end{bmatrix}</math>
::<math>\alpha_k = \operatorname{argmin}_{\alpha\in A_k} \|G_k \alpha\|_2, \quad \text{where}\;A_k = \{\alpha = (\alpha_0, \dots, \alpha_{m_k}) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_k+1} : \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}\alpha_i = 1\}</math>
::<math>x_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i f_{k-m_k+i}</math>

where the matrix–vector multiplication <math>G_k \alpha = \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha)_i g_{k-m_k+i}</math>, and <math>(\alpha)_i</math> is the <math>i</math>th element of <math>\alpha</math>. Conventional stopping criteria can be used to end the iterations of the method. For example, iterations can be stopped when <math>\|x_{k+1} - x_k\|</math> falls under a prescribed tolerance, or when the residual <math>g(x_k)</math> falls under a prescribed tolerance.<ref name="Quarteroni-Sacco" />

With respect to the standard fixed-point iteration, the method has been found to converge faster and be more robust, and in some cases avoid the divergence of the fixed-point sequence.<ref name="Walker2011" /><ref name="Fang2009" />

=== Derivation ===

For the solution <math>x^*</math>, we know that <math>f(x^*) = x^*</math>, which is equivalent to saying that <math>g(x^*) = \vec{0}</math>. We can therefore rephrase the problem as an optimization problem where we want to minimize <math>\|g(x)\|_2</math>.

Instead of going directly from <math>x_k</math> to <math>x_{k+1}</math> by choosing <math>x_{k+1} = f(x_k)</math> as in [[fixed-point iteration]], let's consider an intermediate point <math>x'_{k+1}</math> that we choose to be the [[linear combination]] <math>x'_{k+1} = X_k \alpha_k </math>, where the coefficient vector <math>\alpha_k \in A_k</math>, and <math>X_k = \begin{bmatrix} x_{k-m_k} & \dots & x_k \end{bmatrix}</math> is the matrix containing the last <math>m_k+1</math> points, and choose <math>x'_{k+1}</math> such that it minimizes <math>\|g(x'_{k+1})\|_2</math>. Since the elements in <math>\alpha_k</math> sum to one, we can make the first order approximation 

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
g(X_k\alpha_k) &= g\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m_k} (\alpha_k)_i x_{k-m_k+i}\right) \\
&\approx \sum_{i=0}^{m_k} (\alpha_k)_i g(x_{k-m_k+i}) \\
&=\; G_k\alpha_k
\end{aligned}
</math>

and our problem becomes to find the <math>\alpha</math> that minimizes <math>\|G_k\alpha\|_2</math>. After having found <math>\alpha_k</math>, we could in principle calculate <math>x'_{k+1}</math>.

However, since <math>f</math> is designed to bring a point closer to <math>x^*</math>, <math>f(x'_{k+1})</math> is probably closer to <math>x^*</math> than <math>x'_{k+1}</math> is, so it makes sense to choose <math>x_{k+1}=f(x'_{k+1})</math> rather than <math>x_{k+1}=x'_{k+1}</math>. Furthermore, since the elements in <math>\alpha_k</math> sum to one, we can make the first order approximation 

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
f(x'_{k+1}) &= f\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i x_{k-m_k+i}\right)  \\
&\approx \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i f(x_{k-m_k+i}) \\
 &= \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i f_{k-m_k+i} \, .
\end{aligned}
</math>

We therefore choose

<math>x_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i f_{k-m_k+i}</math>.

=== Solution of the minimization problem ===
At each iteration of the algorithm, the constrained [[optimization]] problem <math>\operatorname{argmin}\|G_k \alpha\|_2</math>, subject to <math>\alpha\in A_k</math> needs to be solved. The problem can be recast in several equivalent formulations,<ref name="Walker2011" /> yielding different solution methods which may result in a more convenient implementation:

* defining the matrices <math>\mathcal{G}_k = \begin{bmatrix} g_{k-m_k+1} - g_{k-m_k} & \dots & g_{k} - g_{k-1}\end{bmatrix}</math> and <math>\mathcal{X}_k = \begin{bmatrix} x_{k-m_k+1} - x_{k-m_k} & \dots & x_{k} - x_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}</math>, solve <math>\gamma_k = \operatorname{argmin}_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{m_k}}\|g_k - \mathcal{G}_k\gamma\|_2</math>, and set <math>x_{k+1} = x_k + g_k - (\mathcal{X}_k + \mathcal{G}_k)\gamma_k</math>;<ref name="Walker2011" /><ref name="Fang2009">{{cite journal |last1=Fang |first1=Haw-ren |last2=Saad |first2=Yousef |title=Two classes of multisecant methods for nonlinear acceleration |journal=Numerical Linear Algebra with Applications |date=March 2009 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=197–221 |doi=10.1002/nla.617}}</ref>
* solve <math>\theta_k = \{(\theta_k)_i\}_{i = 1}^{m_k} = \operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m_k}}\left\|g_k + \sum_{i=1}^{m_k}\theta_i(g_{k-i} - g_k)\right\|_2</math>, then set <math>x_{k+1} = x_k + g_k + \sum_{j = 1}^{m_k}(\theta_k)_j(x_{k-j} - x_k + g_{k-j} - g_k)</math>.<ref name="Anderson1965" />

For both choices, the optimization problem is in the form of an unconstrained [[linear least-squares]] problem, which can be solved by standard methods including [[QR decomposition]]<ref name="Walker2011" /> and [[singular value decomposition]],<ref name="Fang2009" /> possibly including regularization techniques to deal with [[rank (linear algebra)|rank deficiencies]] and [[condition number|conditioning]] issues in the optimization problem. Solving the least-squares problem by solving the [[Numerical methods for linear least squares#Inverting the matrix of the normal equations|normal equations]] is generally not advisable due to potential [[numerical stability|numerical instabilities]] and generally high computational cost.<ref name="Fang2009" />

Stagnation in the method (i.e. subsequent iterations with the same value, <math>x_{k+1} = x_k</math>) causes the method to break down, due to the singularity of the least-squares problem. Similarly, near-stagnation (<math>x_{k+1}\approx x_k</math>) results in bad conditioning of the least squares problem. Moreover, the choice of the parameter <math>m</math> might be relevant in determining the conditioning of the least-squares problem, as discussed [[#Choice of m|below]].<ref name="Walker2011" />

=== Relaxation ===
The algorithm can be modified introducing a variable relaxation parameter (or mixing parameter) <math>\beta_k > 0</math>.<ref name="Anderson1965" /><ref name="Walker2011" /><ref name="Fang2009" /> At each step, compute the new iterate as <math display="block">x_{k+1} = (1 - \beta_k)\sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i x_{k-m_k+i} + \beta_k \sum_{i=0}^{m_k}(\alpha_k)_i f(x_{k-m_k+i})\;.</math>The choice of <math>\beta_k</math> is crucial to the convergence properties of the method; in principle, <math>\beta_k</math> might vary at each iteration, although it is often chosen to be constant.<ref name="Fang2009" />

=== Choice of {{mvar|m}} ===
The parameter <math>m</math> determines how much information from previous iterations is used to compute the new iteration <math>x_{k+1}</math>. On the one hand, if <math>m</math> is chosen to be too small, too little information is used and convergence may be undesirably slow. On the other hand, if <math>m</math> is too large, information from old iterations may be retained for too many subsequent iterations, so that again convergence may be slow.<ref name="Walker2011" /> Moreover, the choice of <math>m</math> affects the size of the optimization problem. A too large value of <math>m</math> may worsen the conditioning of the least squares problem and the cost of its solution.<ref name="Walker2011" /> In general, the particular problem to be solved determines the best choice of the <math>m</math> parameter.<ref name="Walker2011" />

=== Choice of {{mvar|m}}{{sub|{{mvar|k}}}} ===
With respect to the algorithm described above, the choice of <math>m_k</math> at each iteration can be modified. One possibility is to choose <math>m_k = k</math> for each iteration <math>k</math> (sometimes referred to as Anderson acceleration without truncation).<ref name="Walker2011" /> This way, every new iteration <math>x_{k+1}</math> is computed using all the previously computed iterations. A more sophisticated technique is based on choosing <math>m_k</math> so as to maintain a small enough conditioning for the least-squares problem.<ref name="Walker2011" />

== Relations to other classes of methods ==
[[Newton's method]] can be applied to the solution of <math>f(x) - x = 0</math> to compute a fixed point of <math>f(x)</math> with quadratic convergence. However, such method requires the evaluation of the exact derivative of <math>f(x)</math>, which can be very costly.<ref name="Fang2009" /> Approximating the derivative by means of [[finite difference]]s is a possible alternative, but it requires multiple evaluations of <math>f(x)</math> at each iteration, which again can become very costly. Anderson acceleration requires only one evaluation of the function <math>f(x)</math> per iteration, and no evaluation of its derivative. On the other hand, the convergence of an Anderson-accelerated fixed point sequence is still linear in general.<ref name="Evans2020">{{cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=Claire |last2=Pollock |first2=Sara |last3=Rebholz |first3=Leo G. |last4=Xiao |first4=Mengying |title=A Proof That Anderson Acceleration Improves the Convergence Rate in Linearly Converging Fixed-Point Methods (But Not in Those Converging Quadratically) |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |date=20 February 2020 |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=788–810 |doi=10.1137/19M1245384|arxiv=1810.08455 }}</ref>

Several authors have pointed out similarities between the Anderson acceleration scheme and other methods for the solution of non-linear equations. In particular:
* Eyert<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eyert |first1=V. |title=A Comparative Study on Methods for Convergence Acceleration of Iterative Vector Sequences |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |date=March 1996 |volume=124 |issue=2 |pages=271–285 |doi=10.1006/jcph.1996.0059}}</ref> and Fang and Saad<ref name="Fang2009" /> interpreted the algorithm within the class of [[quasi-Newton method|quasi-Newton]] and multisecant methods, that generalize the well known [[secant method]], for the solution of the non-linear equation <math>g(x) = 0</math>; they also showed how the scheme can be seen as a method in the [[Broyden's method|Broyden class]];<ref name="Broyden1965">{{cite journal |last1=Broyden |first1=C. G. |title=A class of methods for solving nonlinear simultaneous equations |journal=Mathematics of Computation |date=1965 |volume=19 |issue=92 |pages=577–593 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0198670-6|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* Walker and Ni<ref name="Walker2011" /><ref name="Ni2009">{{cite thesis |last=Ni |first=Peng |date=November 2009 |title=Anderson Acceleration of Fixed-point Iteration with Applications to Electronic Structure Computations |type=PhD}}</ref> showed that the Anderson acceleration scheme is equivalent to the [[GMRES]] method in the case of linear problems (i.e. the problem of finding a solution to <math>A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}</math> for some [[square matrix]] <math>A</math>), and can thus be seen as a generalization of GMRES to the non-linear case; a similar result was found by Washio and Oosterlee.<ref name="Washio1997">{{cite journal |last1=Oosterlee |first1=C. W. |last2=Washio |first2=T. |title=Krylov Subspace Acceleration of Nonlinear Multigrid with Application to Recirculating Flows |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |date=January 2000 |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=1670–1690 |doi=10.1137/S1064827598338093}}</ref>

Moreover, several equivalent or nearly equivalent methods have been independently developed by other authors,<ref name="Washio1997" /><ref name="Pulay1980">{{cite journal |last1=Pulay |first1=Péter |title=Convergence acceleration of iterative sequences. the case of scf iteration |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |date=July 1980 |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=393–398 |doi=10.1016/0009-2614(80)80396-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pulay |first1=P. |title=ImprovedSCF convergence acceleration |journal=Journal of Computational Chemistry |date=1982 |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=556–560 |doi=10.1002/jcc.540030413}}</ref><ref name="Carlson1998">{{cite journal |last1=Carlson |first1=Neil N. |last2=Miller |first2=Keith |title=Design and Application of a Gradient-Weighted Moving Finite Element Code I: in One Dimension |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |date=May 1998 |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=728–765 |doi=10.1137/S106482759426955X}}</ref><ref name="Miller2005">{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Keith |title=Nonlinear Krylov and moving nodes in the method of lines |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |date=November 2005 |volume=183 |issue=2 |pages=275–287 |doi=10.1016/j.cam.2004.12.032|doi-access= }}</ref> although most often in the context of some specific application of interest rather than as a general method for fixed point equations.

== Example MATLAB implementation ==

The following is an example implementation in [[MATLAB]] language of the Anderson acceleration scheme for finding the fixed-point of the function <math>f(x) = \sin(x) + \arctan(x)</math>. Notice that:
* the optimization problem was solved in the form <math>\gamma_k = \operatorname{argmin}_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{m_k}}\|g_k - \mathcal{G}_k\gamma\|_2</math> using QR decomposition;
* the computation of the QR decomposition is sub-optimal: indeed, at each iteration a single column is added to the matrix <math>\mathcal{G}_k</math>, and possibly a single column is removed; this fact can be exploited to efficiently update the QR decomposition with less computational effort;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Daniel |first1=J. W. |last2=Gragg |first2=W. B. |last3=Kaufman |first3=L. |last4=Stewart |first4=G. W. |title=Reorthogonalization and stable algorithms for updating the Gram-Schmidt $QR$ factorization |journal=Mathematics of Computation |date=October 1976 |volume=30 |issue=136 |pages=772 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1976-0431641-8|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* the algorithm can be made more memory-efficient by storing only the latest few iterations and residuals, if the whole vector of iterations <math>x_k</math> is not needed;
* the code is straightforwardly generalized to the case of a vector-valued <math>f(x)</math>.

<syntaxhighlight lang="matlab">
f = @(x) sin(x) + atan(x); % Function whose fixed point is to be computed.
x0 = 1; % Initial guess.

k_max = 100; % Maximum number of iterations.
tol_res = 1e-6; % Tolerance on the residual.
m = 3; % Parameter m.

x = [x0, f(x0)]; % Vector of iterates x.
g = f(x) - x; % Vector of residuals.

G_k = g(2) - g(1); % Matrix of increments in residuals.
X_k = x(2) - x(1); % Matrix of increments in x.

k = 2;
while k < k_max && abs(g(k)) > tol_res
    m_k = min(k, m);
 
    % Solve the optimization problem by QR decomposition.
    [Q, R] = qr(G_k);
    gamma_k = R \ (Q' * g(k));
 
    % Compute new iterate and new residual.
    x(k + 1) = x(k) + g(k) - (X_k + G_k) * gamma_k;
    g(k + 1) = f(x(k + 1)) - x(k + 1);
 
    % Update increment matrices with new elements.
    X_k = [X_k, x(k + 1) - x(k)];
    G_k = [G_k, g(k + 1) - g(k)];
 
    n = size(X_k, 2);
    if n > m_k
        X_k = X_k(:, n - m_k + 1:end);
        G_k = G_k(:, n - m_k + 1:end);
    end
 
    k = k + 1;
end

% Prints result: Computed fixed point 2.013444 after 9 iterations
fprintf("Computed fixed point %f after %d iterations\n", x(end), k);
</syntaxhighlight>
